title: Finance & Accounts Adventure 1: Financial Statements
welcome_lead: Today you'll read a profit & loss account, a balance sheet and a cash flow statement.
meta_desc: Business Management Finance: profit and loss, balance sheet structure, cash flow statement.
final_note: You read the three core financial statements and distinguished profit from cash.

concepts.def: Money in and out over a period

walkthroughs.body_html:
The P&L tracks performance over a period.

Revenue − Cost of Sales = Gross Profit.
Gross Profit − Expenses = Operating (Net) Profit.
Operating Profit − Interest − Tax = Profit for the Year.

It explains what the firm earned, not how much cash it holds.

The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date.

Assets (fixed + current) = Liabilities (long-term + current) + Equity.

Current assets: cash, debtors, stock. Current liabilities: creditors, overdraft. Their difference is working capital — the cushion for daily trading.

A firm can be profitable but insolvent — paper profits, no cash.

The cash flow statement classifies cash by operating, investing and financing activities.

Improving cash flow: extend creditor terms, chase debtors, reduce stock, lease not buy.

mcqs.q: Does positive cash flow prove a business is profitable?
options: No — cash can rise from loans, share issues or selling assets while the firm trades at a loss; profitability and liquidity are different measures.
The balance sheet records employee attendance.
Money piling up in the bank means the business must be making profit.
Cash flow is simply profit after tax.
No — depreciation spreads the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life in the accounts; no cash leaves the business when the charge is made.
Charging depreciation drains the bank account each year.
